citation: Simoes MDSMP, Proença NL, Lauria VT, do Nascimento MB, Padovani RDC, Dourado VZ. (2026). Effects of Using a Smartphone App Combined With Behavior Change Techniques on the Level of Physical Activity Among Adults and Older Adults: Sequential Multiple Assignment Randomized Trial. Journal of Medical Internet Research, 28, e73388.
population: Adults and older adults; N=53; mean age 44.0 ± 12.7 years
adherence_problem: Physical-activity engagement declines over time; initial nonresponse may require treatment adaptation [study rationale]
intervention: Initial randomization to app + tailored messages, app + tailored messages + gamification I, or educational control; at week 6 intervention participants were classified as responders/nonresponders and nonresponders could receive an adapted second-stage package including gamification II; after week 12 participants were advised to continue app step monitoring without direct researcher intervention
BCT_or_mechanism: Self-monitoring; individual goal setting; tailored messages/feedback; graded tasks; virtual badges/rewards; ranking/social comparison; social support; educational instruction
duration: 24 weeks total: 12-week active multistage intervention + 12-week follow-up
outcome: Accelerometer-measured daily steps, sedentary behavior and MVPA
result_and_DOI: Group 1 increased daily steps across assessments and maintained gains at follow-up; responder trajectories were favorable; control step counts declined at follow-up. Do not attribute the result to gamification alone. DOI: https://doi.org/10.2196/73388
phase_structure: 0–6 weeks initial treatment → week-6 response classification → 6–12 weeks adapted second stage → 12–24 weeks self-directed follow-up
shared_backbone_or_active_comparator: Educational-information control; intervention arms share app-based monitoring but differ in tailored messages/gamification and response-triggered escalation
adaptation_or_personalization: Response-adaptive sequencing (SMART); treatment changes depend on week-6 step-count response
engagement_or_exposure: Groups 1 and 2 had 63% and 47% responders at week 6; only one participant explored unassigned app gamification features; follow-up continued app monitoring without direct researcher interference
maintenance_interpretation: sustained gain — favorable step-count trajectory persisted into follow-up for group 1/responders, while control declined

citation: Sagelv EH, Manskow US, Antypas K, Morseth B, Aksetøy ILA, Nes BM, Gagnon MP, Zanaboni P. (2025). Online interventions to increase physical activity levels in self-reported inactive adults: the ONWARDS randomised controlled trial. BMJ Open Sport & Exercise Medicine.
population: Self-reported inactive adults; N=183; age 22–55 years
target_behavior: MVPA; light PA; total PA; steps; sedentary time
adherence_problem: Long-term effectiveness and maintenance of digitally supported physical activity [study rationale]
intervention: Group A: activity tracker + PAI app; Group B: A + home-based online training; Group C: B + closed social-media peer support
BCT_or_mechanism: Self-monitoring; personalized feedback via PAI; goal/reference metric; structured home exercise; peer/social support
duration: 18 months with assessments at 6, 12 and 18 months
outcome: ActiGraph-measured MVPA, light PA, total PA, steps and sedentary time
result_and_DOI: No sustained group-by-time advantage across the increasingly intensive packages; Group C showed a temporary 6-month MVPA advantage, then groups converged; overall MVPA declined over 18 months. DOI: https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjsem-2023-001816
phase_structure: continuous 18-month exposure with long-term repeated follow-up
shared_backbone_or_active_comparator: All arms received tracker + PAI app; B added online training; C added online training + peer support; no inactive/no-intervention control
adaptation_or_personalization: Static personalization via PAI metric; no response-adaptive sequencing
engagement_or_exposure: Accelerometer follow-up completeness fell to 42.7% at 18 months; fully web-based delivery limited control over component use
maintenance_interpretation: attenuation — temporary early advantage from added peer-support layer did not persist; groups converged while overall MVPA declined

citation: Vos AL, de Bruijn GJ, Klein MCA, Boerman SC, Stuber JM, Smit EG. (2025). Effectiveness of a Just-In-Time Adaptive App to Increase Daily Steps: An RCT. American Journal of Preventive Medicine, 68(1).
population: Adults in low-socioeconomic-position neighborhoods in the Netherlands; N=176; mean age ≈56 years; 76% female
adherence_problem: Need for context-sensitive, individually relevant support to promote walking [study rationale]
intervention: Intervention: step-counter app + dynamically tailored just-in-time coaching delivered through push notifications; control: step-counter app only
BCT_or_mechanism: Self-monitoring; individually tailored feedback; preference-sensitive walking advice; context-aware suggestions linked to suitable walking locations
duration: 6 or 12 months depending on municipality/funding period; questionnaires at 3, 6 and 12 months where applicable
result_and_DOI: No significant average intervention effect on steps over time; perceived usefulness significantly moderated the intervention effect, with more favorable response among participants reporting greater usefulness. DOI: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.amepre.2024.09.010
phase_structure: continuous exposure with longitudinal follow-up; not a clean acquisition→maintenance design
shared_backbone_or_active_comparator: Both groups received a step-counter/self-monitoring app; incremental contrast was the JITAI coaching layer
adaptation_or_personalization: Contextual/JITAI tailoring based on participant/context information and preferences
engagement_or_exposure: About 30% of possible daily step observations were present; missingness increased over time; actual reading of coaching messages could not be verified
maintenance_interpretation: no maintenance advantage — no average incremental step benefit over active self-monitoring control; experienced usefulness modified response

citation: Brickwood KJ, Ahuja KDK, Watson G, O'Brien J, Williams AD. (2021). Effects of Activity Tracker Use With Health Professional Support or Telephone Counseling on Maintenance of Physical Activity and Health Outcomes in Older Adults: Randomized Controlled Trial. JMIR mHealth and uHealth, 9(1), e18686.
population: Older adults >60 years; N=117; mean age 72.4 ± 6.4 years; participants had just completed a 12-week individualized community exercise program
target_behavior: Daily steps; nonstepping time; physical activity maintenance
adherence_problem: Maintaining physical activity after completion of a structured exercise program [study rationale]
intervention: Activity tracker + smartphone app + accredited exercise-physiologist support versus telephone counseling versus usual care
BCT_or_mechanism: Self-monitoring; goal setting; feedback; motivational interviewing / self-efficacy support
duration: 12 months with assessments at 3, 6 and 12 months
outcome: ActivPAL-measured daily steps and nonstepping time; Active Australia Survey self-report
result_and_DOI: Tracker and telephone-counseling groups broadly maintained daily steps while usual care declined; between-group differences were not uniformly significant. DOI: https://doi.org/10.2196/18686
phase_structure: post-program maintenance trial beginning immediately after a prior 12-week exercise intervention
shared_backbone_or_active_comparator: All participants entered after the same prior community exercise program; randomized maintenance support was tracker+AEP versus telephone counseling versus usual care
adaptation_or_personalization: No adaptive sequencing; support was personalized/professional but not JITAI
engagement_or_exposure: Tracker group wore the device on about 84% of available days; telephone group received about 12 calls averaging 11.1 minutes
maintenance_interpretation: preserved behavior — tracker and telephone-support groups largely maintained steps rather than showing clear additional gains

citation: Yoshimura E, Tajiri E, Michiwaki R, Matsumoto N, Hatamoto Y, Tanaka S. (2022). Long-term Effects of the Use of a Step Count–Specific Smartphone App on Physical Activity and Weight Loss: Randomized Controlled Clinical Trial. JMIR mHealth and uHealth, 10(10), e35628.
population: Adults aged 30–60 years; N=109; mean age 47 ± 8 years
adherence_problem: Long-duration support for increasing physical activity during a weight-management program [study rationale]
intervention: App group used a step-count/ranking smartphone app; both groups received a 1-hour PA/weight-loss lecture, daily self-weighing instructions, monthly advisory emails and periodic feedback
BCT_or_mechanism: Step self-monitoring; group ranking/social comparison; goal setting (+1000 steps/day); shared education, self-weighing, motivational emails and feedback
outcome: Triaxial-accelerometer step count and MVPA; body weight measured separately
result_and_DOI: App group showed a more favorable step-count trajectory, especially on weekends; increased PA did not produce additional weight loss versus control. DOI: https://doi.org/10.2196/35628
phase_structure: continuous 32-week active exposure; not automatically a maintenance phase
shared_backbone_or_active_comparator: Both groups received lecture, self-weighing, monthly motivational emails and periodic feedback; incremental contrast was daily app step/rank checking
adaptation_or_personalization: No adaptive sequencing; static app-based self-monitoring/ranking
engagement_or_exposure: App checking at least daily was about 80.1% through 12 weeks and 73.6% during weeks 12–32; dropout at 32 weeks was low
maintenance_interpretation: not a maintenance design — long-duration active exposure showed PA benefit without additional weight-loss benefit
